entry: Spherical model of [[Earth]], another celestial body, or the [[Celestial sphere|celestial sphere]]. Globes serve purposes similar to those of [[Map|maps]] but, unlike maps, do not distort the surface they portray except to scale it down. A terrestrial globe shows landmasses, water bodies, nations, major cities and the network of latitude and longitude lines, sometimes with raised relief showing mountains. A celestial globe shows notable stars and divides the sphere into [[Constellation|constellations]]. The word comes from Latin *globus* ("sphere"). The first known mention of a globe, by Strabo, describes the Globe of Crates from about 150 BC. The oldest surviving terrestrial globe is the Erdapfel, made by Martin Behaim in 1492, and the oldest surviving celestial globe sits atop the Farnese Atlas, carved in the 2nd century [[Roman Empire]].

Brand of polymer-framed semi-automatic pistols made by Austrian firm Glock GmbH. Its first pistol, later sold as the Glock 17, entered Austrian military and police service in 1982 after outperforming rivals in reliability and safety tests. The "Safe Action" system has three internal safeties: trigger, firing pin and drop. Glock pistols serve militaries and police in at least 48 countries, including the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]]. In 2024 [[Minnesota]] and [[New Jersey]] sued over illegal aftermarket auto sears, known as "Glock switches," that convert pistols into machine pistols, and [[California]] passed legislation in 2025 aimed at forcing design changes to prevent such conversions.

American journalist and social movement activist. A leader of second-wave [[Feminism|feminism]] in the United States in the late 1960s and early 1970s, she was a columnist for *New York* magazine and co-founded *Ms.* magazine. Her 1969 article "After Black Power, Women's Liberation" brought her national attention. In 1971 she co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus, which provided training and support for women seeking elected and appointed office. In 2005 she co-founded the Women's Media Center with [[Jane Fonda]] and Robin Morgan. In 2015 she traveled from [[Pyongyang]] to South Korea with two Nobel Peace laureates, crossing the Korean Demilitarized Zone.

American artist, author, actress, fashion designer, heiress and socialite. Born in [[Manhattan]], she was the daughter of railroad heir Reginald Claypoole Vanderbilt, of the [[Vanderbilt family]]. In 1934 her mother and her aunt, the sculptor Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, each sought custody of her in a case dubbed the "trial of the century," which Whitney won. In the 1970s Vanderbilt launched a line of fashions, perfumes and household goods bearing her name, and she was an early developer of designer blue jeans.

Deposition of [[James II of England|King James II of England]] in November 1688. William III of Orange, the Dutch husband of James's daughter Mary II, had been invited by English opponents of the king and landed in Devon with a Dutch army on 5 November 1688. As William advanced on London, James's army disintegrated, and James fled to France in December. In April 1689 a Convention made William and Mary joint monarchs of England and Ireland. The settlement formally established [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] in Britain. The revolt ignited [[Jacobitism]], the movement to restore the exiled Stuarts, which persisted into the late 18th century.

Optical property of a surface that reflects light in a specular (mirror-like) direction. Gloss is one of the main parameters used to describe an object's visual appearance. Apparent gloss depends on the amount of specular reflection compared with diffuse reflection, the light scattered in other directions. The factors that affect gloss are the [[Refractive index|refractive index]] of the material, the angle of incident light and the surface texture. Smooth surfaces, such as highly polished objects or coatings with finely dispersed pigments, look shiny, while rough surfaces scatter light and appear dull. Metals reflect strongly at any angle, whereas non-metallic materials reflect more light at greater illumination angles. The earliest studies of gloss perception are attributed to Leonard R. Ingersoll, who in 1914 examined the effect of gloss on paper.

Ceremonial county of South West England. It is bordered by Herefordshire, Worcestershire, Warwickshire, Oxfordshire and Wiltshire, by [[Bristol]] and [[Somerset]] to the south-west, and by the Welsh county of Monmouthshire to the west. The largest settlement is the city of Gloucester. The predominantly rural county covers 3,150 sq km (1,220 sq mi) and had an estimated population of 975,712 in 2024. The River Severn bisects it, and the east of the county contains most of the Cotswolds. Bristol became an independent county in 1373, when it was the third-largest city in England.

Garment covering the hand, with separate sheaths for each finger and the thumb. Gloves protect the hands against cold or heat, friction, abrasion, chemicals and disease. They are made of cloth, knitted or felted [[Wool|wool]], [[Leather|leather]], rubber, latex, [[Silk|silk]] and, in mail, metal. Fingerless gloves leave the fingers uncovered where dexterity is needed, and [[Cycling|cycling]] gloves are usually fingerless. Health care workers often wear disposable latex, nitrile or vinyl gloves, and police officers wear them at crime scenes to avoid destroying evidence. An ancient Egyptian tomb of the 5th dynasty depicts gloves. They reached their greatest elaboration in the 16th century, when [[Elizabeth I]] set the fashion for wearing them richly embroidered and jeweled.

Simple sugar and the most abundant monosaccharide in the biosphere. Its molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆, and it is the most important energy source in all organisms. Plants and most algae make glucose by [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], using energy from sunlight to combine water and carbon dioxide, and plants use it to build [[Cellulose|cellulose]], the most abundant carbohydrate in the world. Living organisms use it to replenish [[Adenosine triphosphate|adenosine triphosphate]] (ATP) inside cells. Plants store glucose as starch and animals store it as [[Glycogen|glycogen]], and it circulates in animal blood as blood sugar. Intravenous glucose solution is on the [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines. Glucose was first isolated from raisins in 1747 by Andreas Marggraf.

Massless [[Elementary particle|elementary particle]] that mediates the [[Strong interaction|strong interaction]] between quarks. The gluon is a vector boson with a spin of 1 that binds quarks into groups called hadrons, such as protons and neutrons, as described by [[Quantum chromodynamics|quantum chromodynamics]]. Unlike [[Photon|photons]], which carry no electric charge, gluons carry color charge themselves, making the theory harder to analyze than [[Quantum electrodynamics|quantum electrodynamics]]. There are eight independent types of gluon. Experiments limit the gluon's rest mass to less than a few MeV/c². [[Murray Gell-Mann]] used the term in a 1962 paper, suggesting the glue that holds the nucleus together. Richard Feynman grouped quarks and gluons under the name partons.

Sugar alcohol with the formula C₃H₅(OH)₃. It is a colorless, odorless, sweet-tasting, viscous liquid that is miscible with water and hygroscopic. Glycerol forms the backbone of glycerides, including the triglycerides of animal fats and vegetable oils, from which it is obtained. Saponification of these fats with [[Sodium hydroxide|sodium hydroxide]] yields glycerol and [[Soap|soap]]. Commercial glycerine is typically 95% pure. Since about 2010, biofuel production has created a large surplus of glycerol. It is used as a sweetener in food and a humectant in pharmaceuticals, and as a precursor to [[Nitroglycerin|nitroglycerin]]; during [[World War II]] synthetic production became a national defense priority for that reason.

Multibranched polysaccharide of [[Glucose|glucose]] that serves as an energy store in animals, fungi and bacteria. It is the main storage form of glucose in the human body. In humans it is made and stored mainly in the [[Liver|liver]] and skeletal muscle. The liver can hold 5–6% of its fresh weight as glycogen, roughly 100–120 grams in an adult, while skeletal muscle holds 1–2% of its mass and uses its store mainly for its own energy. Liver glycogen supplies glucose to the rest of the body, particularly the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]], and about 4 grams of glucose circulate in human blood at all times. Glycogen is an analogue of [[Starch|starch]] but is more extensively branched and compact, forming an energy reserve that can be mobilized quickly.

Metabolic pathway that converts [[Glucose|glucose]] into pyruvate, usually in the cytosol of cells. The energy released forms adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and NADH through ten enzyme-catalyzed reactions. The pathway has an investment phase, in which ATP is consumed, and a yield phase, in which more ATP is produced than was consumed. Under low-oxygen conditions it is the only pathway in eukaryotes that can generate ATP, so many organisms use [[Fermentation|fermentation]] to recycle NAD⁺ and keep glycolysis running. Its most common form, the Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway, was discovered by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and Jakub Karol Parnas. [[Louis Pasteur]] studied yeast fermentation in the 1850s, and in the 1890s Eduard Buchner showed that a non-living yeast extract could convert glucose to ethanol.

[[Email]] service provided by [[Google]]. It is the largest email service in the world, with 1.8 billion users, accessible through a web browser, mobile apps or third-party clients using POP and IMAP. Launched as a beta version in 2004, it left beta in 2009. Free accounts include 15 gigabytes of storage shared with Google Drive and Google Photos. Messages suspected of being spam, [[Malware|malware]] or [[Phishing|phishing]] are moved from the inbox to a separate folder. Its early adoption of Ajax made it notable among web developers.

Infraphylum of jawed vertebrates, from Ancient Greek *gnathos* ("jaw") and *stoma* ("mouth"). Gnathostomes number roughly 60,000 species, which make up 99% of living vertebrates, including all bony fishes, cartilaginous fishes and [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]]. Most retain ancestral traits such as true teeth, a stomach and paired appendages such as fins or limbs. Traditionally the group is divided into [[Chondrichthyes|cartilaginous fish]], the extinct [[Placoderm|placoderms]] and Teleostomi, which includes bony fishes, birds, mammals, reptiles and amphibians. The jaw is likely a product of bending the first pair of gill arches. Undisputed gnathostome fossils appear in the early [[Silurian]] and are abundant by the start of the [[Devonian]]. Its sister group is the [[Agnatha|jawless fish]].

Common high-grade [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic rock]] with a banded texture. It forms when [[Igneous rock|igneous]] or [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rocks]] are subjected to high temperature and pressure, ranging from 2 to 15 kbar, sometimes more, and temperatures over 300 °C. Gneiss nearly always shows alternating darker and lighter bands and lacks a distinct cleavage. The darker bands contain more mafic minerals, rich in magnesium and iron, while the lighter bands contain more felsic minerals such as [[Feldspar|feldspar]] and [[Quartz|quartz]]. Gneisses are common in the ancient crust of continental shields, and some of the oldest rocks on Earth are gneisses, such as the Acasta Gneiss.

Umbrella term for religious and philosophical systems of early Christian sects and other faiths. These systems fully developed by the mid-second century and emphasized personal spiritual knowledge (*gnosis*) above the authority of organized religious institutions. The Gnostic worldview distinguished a hidden supreme being from a flawed [[Demiurge|demiurge]], identified in the Hebrew Bible with [[Yahweh]], who created the material universe. Salvation came through direct knowledge of one's own divine origin, attained by mystical or esoteric insight. Early Church Fathers denounced Gnostic ideas as [[Heresy|heresy]], and efforts to destroy Gnostic texts were largely successful. Interest revived after the 1945 discovery of the Nag Hammadi library in Egypt. Since the 1990s, scholars have debated whether "Gnosticism" is a form of early Christianity, an artificial category created to label heresies, or a distinct religious tradition.

Abstract strategy [[Board game|board game]] for two players, invented in [[China]] more than 2,500 years ago. Players alternately place black and white stones on the intersections of a grid, aiming to enclose more territory than the opponent. The standard board has a 19×19 grid containing 361 points. Captured stones are removed from the board. The winner is decided by counting surrounded territory and captured stones, plus komi, points added to the score of the player with the white stones as compensation for playing second. Go is believed to be the oldest board game still played. A 2016 survey of the International Go Federation's 75 member nations found over 46 million people who know how to play, most of them in [[East Asia]]. Compared with [[Chess]], Go has a larger board and, on average, many more alternatives per move.

State on the southwestern coast of [[India]]. Goa was an overseas territory of the [[Portugal|Portuguese]] empire for approximately 451 years until its annexation by India in December 1961. Panaji is the capital. The [[Western Ghats]] separate it from the Deccan highlands, and the [[Arabian Sea]] forms its western coast. It is India's smallest state by area and has the second-highest GDP per capita among Indian states. It ranks highest among Indian states in the [[Human Development Index|Human Development Index]]. Old Goa, considered one of the greatest cities of Asia in the 16th century, was abandoned in the 19th century after disease outbreaks.

Domesticated caprine mammal kept as [[Livestock|livestock]]. The domestic goat (*Capra hircus*) descends from the wild goat of Southwest Asia and Eastern Europe. It was one of the first animals to be domesticated, in Iran around 10,000 years ago. Goats are members of the family [[Bovidae]] and are closely related to [[Sheep|sheep]]. More than 1.1 billion goats lived in the world in 2022, 150 million of them in [[India]]. Goats supply milk, cheese, goatskin, meat and wool. They feature in many myths and religions, from the goats that pulled the chariot of the Norse god [[Thor]] to the goat as a common depiction of [[Satan]] in Christianity. Neolithic farmers herded wild goats for milk and meat, and their dung was used as fuel.

Large cold desert and grassland region in southern [[Mongolia]] and [[China|North China]]. It is the sixth-largest desert in the world, covering about 1,295,000 sq km (500,000 sq mi). The name comes from Mongolian *gov'*, meaning dryland, and much of the Gobi is bare rock rather than sand. Winter temperatures can fall to −40 °C and summer temperatures can reach 45 °C, and an average of about 194 mm of rain falls annually. The region is the source of important fossil finds, including the first dinosaur eggs, 26 of which were uncovered in 1923. Its animals include black-tailed gazelles, marbled polecats, wild [[Bactrian camel|Bactrian camels]] and the Mongolian wild ass.

Suborder of percomorph fishes, many of them called gobies. Gobioidei is by far the largest and most diverse group within Gobiiformes and one of the most diverse groups of ray-finned fishes, with about 2,211 species in seven families. Most are small, marine, bottom-dwelling fishes with large heads and tapered bodies, and roughly 10% live in fresh water. Lacking a gas bladder, most gobioids spend most of their time on or near the bottom. Traditionally classed as a suborder of [[Perciformes]], the group was elevated to an order in the 5th edition of *Fishes of the World* and is again placed as a suborder within an expanded Gobiiformes. The earliest known fossil member is *Carlomonnius*, from the Early Eocene of Italy.

Action-adventure video game franchise, developed by the Santa Monica Studio of [[Sony]]. David Jaffe created the series, which began in 2005 on the [[PlayStation 2]]. It centers on Kratos, a [[Sparta|Spartan]] warrior who becomes the God of War. The Greek games follow his vengeance against the Olympian gods; the Norse games, beginning with *God of War* (2018), follow his redemption alongside his son Atreus. Sony Interactive Entertainment published all but the mobile phone installment. The franchise has sold an estimated 66+ million games, and is PlayStation's most profitable first-party brand.

River of south-central India, second only to the [[Ganges]] in length. It rises near Nashik in Maharashtra, about 80 km from the [[Arabian Sea]], and flows 1,465 km east across the [[Deccan Plateau]] before entering the [[Bay of Bengal]] through a broad delta. Its 312,812 sq km basin covers about 10% of India's area and is the third largest in India, after those of the Ganga and Indus. In length, catchment area and discharge it is the largest river of peninsular India, and it has been called the *Dakshina Ganga* ("Southern Ganges"). Barrages and dams now hold back much of its flow. The delta, with 729 persons per sq km, is nearly twice the Indian average density and faces a substantial flood risk.

Female deity. In some faiths a sacred female figure holds a central place in prayer and worship. [[Shaktism]], one of the three major Hindu sects, holds that the ultimate deity is the Supreme Goddess, Mahamaya, and in [[Vajrayana|Vajrayana Buddhism]] ultimate reality is depicted as two deities in union, symbolizing the non-duality of perfect wisdom and skillful compassion. [[Polytheism|Polytheist]] religions honor many goddesses, often associated with love, beauty, [[Weaving|weaving]], fertility and motherhood, as well as with war, magic, wisdom, fate and justice. [[Inanna]] was the most worshipped goddess in ancient [[Sumer]]. The English word first appeared in [[Middle English]] from about 1350. In monotheistic faiths a female figure may simply be called god, with no need to distinguish gender.
